meta.framing: How do forensic investigators determine whether a corporate data breach was carried out by a malicious insider or by an external intruder using stolen credentials when the initial log evidence appears consistent with both explanations?

notes: Ordering sensitivity, and the required pattern is a FLAT line. Every rung applies only `shuffle_order` or `ordering_only`, both of which are in `EDGE_INVARIANT_CALLS`: reordering sentences moves no edge and a Precedence<->Succession swap compiles to Level-1 `none` either way, so all five rungs build the same Markov network and every relation-graph readout is necessarily equal. Declaring `increase` here (as this ladder did until the 14-family corpus was scored) makes all 15 checks unsatisfiable BY CONSTRUCTION -- measured: 0/15 on each of f004, f007 and f011, with mean_marginal identical to six decimal places across all five rungs. What the ladder can actually test is the CONVERSE of CHAIN: that a readout does NOT move when the prose is reordered but the relations are not. A score that trends here is tracking surface order, not coherence.

atoms.text: Meridian Health Systems discovered that 2.3 million patient records had been exfiltrated from its claims database.
atoms.label: p1

atoms.text: The exfiltration was performed using the valid login credentials of a senior database administrator.
atoms.label: p2

atoms.text: The exfiltration session lasted less than four minutes.
atoms.label: p3

atoms.text: Meridian's legal team argued that the administrator deliberately stole the records.
atoms.label: p4

atoms.text: The administrator's attorney argued that an external attacker had hijacked the account.
atoms.label: p5

atoms.text: The administrator personally carried out the exfiltration.
atoms.label: p6
atoms.factual_note: exhaustive_pair: exactly one of this pair is false

atoms.text: Someone other than the administrator carried out the exfiltration.
atoms.label: p7
atoms.factual_note: exhaustive_pair: exactly one of this pair is false

atoms.text: The session originated from a VPN exit node located in Eastern Europe.
atoms.label: p8

atoms.text: Badge-access records placed the administrator at home during the exfiltration window.
atoms.label: p9

atoms.text: The account was protected by hardware-token multifactor authentication at the time of the breach.
atoms.label: p10

atoms.text: The intruder's session never registered a successful multifactor challenge on the administrator's enrolled device.
atoms.label: p11

atoms.text: No multifactor prompt sent to the administrator's enrolled device was approved during the intruder's session.
atoms.label: p12

atoms.text: The administrator's password was captured through the phishing email.
atoms.label: p13

atoms.text: The administrator's password was reused from an earlier third-party breach.
atoms.label: p14

atoms.text: The state data protection regulator's final report concluded that an external intruder carried out the breach using stolen credentials.
atoms.label: p15

response:
When access logs show a legitimate account doing illegitimate things, the forensic question is not whether the credentials were valid but who was holding them. The breach at Meridian Health Systems shows the method. Meridian discovered that 2.3 million patient records had been exfiltrated from its claims database, a discovery that came only after the exfiltration was performed using the valid login credentials of a senior database administrator. At that first stage the authentication logs could not settle the matter. A valid credential is equally consistent with an employee abusing trusted access and with an outsider replaying a stolen secret. Investigators therefore treat the login itself as the starting point of the analysis rather than its conclusion.

The exfiltration session lasted less than four minutes, and that compressed duration is what caused the operation to run through the administrator's valid credentials rather than through any exploit that would have required slower reconnaissance. Two interpretations quickly hardened into legal positions. Meridian's legal team argued that the administrator deliberately stole the records. By contrast, and despite the use of the administrator's own credentials, the administrator's attorney argued that an external attacker had hijacked the account. Stripped of advocacy, the factual question was binary. Either the administrator personally carried out the exfiltration, or someone other than the administrator carried out the exfiltration. These two accounts cannot both be true, and one of them must hold. The task of the investigation was to gather artifacts that discriminate between them.

Network telemetry was the first such artifact. The session originated from a VPN exit node located in Eastern Europe. Investigators do not treat an exit node as decisive, because an insider can route traffic through a commercial VPN as easily as a foreign operator can. What it does is fix the session to infrastructure that can be subpoenaed and correlated with other timestamps. Physical-presence data supplied one of those correlations. Badge-access records placed the administrator at home during the exfiltration window, which indicates the first of the two accounts, namely that the administrator acted personally. A residence is precisely where an employee could connect remotely through a VPN without generating any on-premises trace.

Authentication controls carry more weight, because they test whether the person holding the password also held the second factor. The account was protected by hardware-token multifactor authentication at the time of the breach. By contrast, the intruder's session never registered a successful multifactor challenge on the administrator's enrolled device. In other words, no multifactor prompt sent to the administrator's enrolled device was approved during the intruder's session. This distinction matters forensically. An insider in possession of the enrolled device would ordinarily leave an approved challenge in the identity-provider logs, whereas an outsider with only the password leaves rejected or unanswered prompts, or none at all.

That absence of any approved prompt caused the administrator's password to be captured through the phishing email that investigators later recovered from the administrator's mailbox. Credential-exposure analysis then broadened the inquiry beyond that single message. At least one of two exposure routes holds, perhaps both: the phishing capture, or the administrator's password having been reused from an earlier third-party breach and circulated in compiled credential dumps. Either route places the secret in hostile hands without any action by the administrator. The state data protection regulator's final report concluded that an external intruder carried out the breach using stolen credentials. That conclusion resolves the tension between the administrator's valid login and the attorney's hijacking defense: the credentials were genuine, but their bearer was not the administrator. The general lesson for investigators is that valid credentials establish only which account was used. Attribution to a person requires converging evidence from network origin, physical location, second-factor telemetry, and the documented exposure history of the secret itself.
